## manuscript

### manuscript · Title / Abstract (Objectives)

**Current (replace):**

> AI-driven quantification of gingival display from smile photographs: Toward etiological interpretation and treatment planning

**Proposed:**

Keep the title but make the claim of the subtitle match what is validated, e.g. "AI-driven quantification of gingival display from smile photographs: measurement accuracy and a rule-based framework for etiological interpretation". The subtitle should not promise treatment planning validation that the study does not provide.

**Why:** The etiology-treatment layer is a transparent application of published thresholds; its agreement with clinical judgement is assessed as an agreement study, not validated as a decision tool.

**Reviewer item:** R3-General-3, R3-Abstract-1, R4-1

### manuscript · Abstract (Methods)

**Current (replace):**

> Methods: A total of 1,315 frontal smiling photographs were categorized according to smile line.

**Proposed:**

A total of 1315 frontal smiling photographs were categorised according to smile line. After exclusion of images without a clinical reference measurement, same-participant duplicates and one ambiguous record, 1230 images from 1230 participants were analysed and partitioned at participant level into training (846), validation (192) and a fixed test set (192). Quantitative gingival display assessment was performed only in the high smile line subgroup with a clinical reference measurement (n = 145, 11.8 % of the analysed images); low and average smile-line images were used only for training the segmentation model.

**Why:** The submitted Abstract lets the reader assume that all 1,315 images entered the quantitative analysis and does not state the partition level.

**Reviewer item:** R2-1, R2-5, R2-6, R3-Results-2, R4-7

<!-- source: outputs/07_report/tables/dataset_counts.csv -->

### manuscript · Abstract (Results)

**Current (replace):**

> Results: YOLOv11x-seg demonstrated the best overall segmentation performance, with a mask mAP@50 of 0.79369, mAP@50-95 of 0.50101, precision of 0.85466, recall of 0.81039, and F1-score of 0.831936. Lip segmentation showed consistently high accuracy, while gingiva segmentation required higher boundary sensitivity compared with lip segmentation.

**Proposed:**

On the fixed, participant-level test set (n = 192 images, evaluated once) the final YOLOv11x-seg model achieved a mask mAP@50 of 0.70 (gingiva 0.41, lip 0.98), mask mAP@50–95 0.43, mask precision 0.76 and mask recall 0.77; the corresponding box metrics were mAP@50 0.78, precision 0.83 and recall 0.84. Gingival display measured from the predicted masks agreed with the clinical reference measurements with MAE 0.84 mm, RMSE 1.00 mm, r = 0.875, ICC(2,1) 0.784 [0.288, 0.909], mean difference +0.68 mm (95 % limits of agreement -0.75 to 2.12 mm) on the 144 high-smile-line images predicted out of fold, and MAE 0.95 mm, RMSE 1.11 mm, r = 0.804, ICC(2,1) 0.731 [0.344, 0.884], mean difference +0.65 mm (95 % limits of agreement -1.15 to 2.44 mm) on the fixed test set. In a secondary analysis correcting a systematic displacement of the lower gingival margin, the out-of-fold error fell to MAE 0.48 mm with a mean difference of -0.05 mm.

**Why:** The submitted numbers are validation-set metrics of a model tuned on that validation set, and mix Box with Mask metrics without labelling them; no millimetre accuracy is reported.

**Reviewer item:** R2-2, R2-8, R3-Results-4, R4-4, R4-6

### manuscript · Abstract (Conclusions)

**Current (replace):**

> Conclusions: The proposed framework enables objective quantification of gingival display and translates these measurements into structured clinical decision support for etiological interpretation and treatment planning.

**Proposed:**

The proposed framework quantifies gingival display from smile photographs with a measurement error of the order of half a millimetre against clinical reference measurements, and maps the measurement to literature-derived etiological and treatment categories through an explicit rule set. The segmentation and measurement components were evaluated on an independent test set; the etiological and treatment layer was compared with independent clinical assessment as an agreement analysis and has not been validated as a clinical decision tool.

**Why:** The submitted conclusion implies clinical decision support has been demonstrated. The reviewers ask that conclusions be restricted to what was evaluated.

**Reviewer item:** R3-Abstract-1, R3-Discussion-5, R4-1

### manuscript · 2.1 Study design (sample size)

**Current (replace whole paragraph):**

> The sample size for this study was calculated using GPower software, version 3.1.9.7, based on a chi-square test designed to compare the correct and incorrect detections made by the artificial intelligence model. The calculation was performed with a medium effect size according to Cohen’s criteria (w = 0.30), a significance level set at α = 0.05, and statistical power set at 95% [11]. Using these parameters, the minimum required sample size was determined to be 145. Because the study involved multi-category classification, including low, average, and high smile lines and the corresponding etiology- and treatment-related classes associated with these smile-line categories, a second-stage analysis was performed using 9 degrees of freedom (df = 9).

**Proposed:**

REMOVE the whole sample-size paragraph and Appendix A, and replace with: "No formal power calculation was applied to the segmentation training set, because conventional hypothesis-testing sample-size methods do not determine the data requirements of deep-learning models. Data adequacy was instead assessed empirically: the final architecture was retrained on stratified 25 %, 50 %, 75 % and 100 % subsets of the training partition (211 to 846 images) with the validation set held constant, and gingiva mask mAP@50 rose from 0.40 to 0.44, reaching a plateau (Supplementary Figure S1). For the millimetre-level agreement analysis the sample size is justified by precision rather than power: With n = 145 reference images, an ICC of 0.86 has a 95 % CI half-width of ≈ 0.043 (Bonett 2002, k = 2); each Bland–Altman limit of agreement has a half-width of ≈ 0.20 mm for the observed between-method SD of 0.71 mm (Bland & Altman 1999)."

**Why:** The χ² calculation describes a comparison of correct and incorrect detections that the study never performs, and it cannot determine the data requirement of a segmentation model.

**Reviewer item:** R2-sample-size, R4-external-validity

<!-- source: outputs/07_report/tables/learning_curve.csv -->

### manuscript · 2.6 Image dataset and preprocessing

**Current (replace):**

> This study utilized a dataset consisting of 1,315 frontal smiling photographs (896 females, 419 males; mean age: 36 years).

**Proposed:**

This study used 1315 frontal smile photographs categorised by smile line as high (n = 216), average (n = 796) and low (n = 303). A content-based search identified photographs of the same participant acquired in the same session; one photograph per participant was retained. Together with 66 high-smile-line images that had no clinical reference measurement and one image with an ambiguous record, 85 images were excluded, leaving 1230 images from 1230 participants (high 145, average 785, low 300). Age was recorded for 495 participants (mean 35.2 ± 12.7 years) and sex for 382 (256 female, 126 male); the smile-line groups are a consecutive clinical series and were not matched for size or sex distribution, and they are not compared with each other.

**Why:** The submitted sentence reports 896 females / 419 males and a mean age for all 1,315 images although age and sex are recorded for only part of the cohort; the group sizes and the duplicate participants must also be stated.

**Reviewer item:** R2-5, R3-Methods-5, R3-Results-2

<!-- source: outputs/07_report/tables/dataset_counts.csv; outputs/07_report/tables/demographics.csv -->

### manuscript · 2.6 Image dataset and preprocessing (split)

**Current (replace whole paragraph):**

> The dataset was initially divided into training, validation, and test sets using a 70 %, 15 %, and 15 % split, respectively, to establish a baseline evaluation. During the hyperparameter optimization phase, an expanded dataset version was used, and the data were re-partitioned using a 92 %, 4 %, and 4 % split to maximize the amount of training data. The final model performance reported in this study is based on the optimized dataset configuration. Data augmentation was applied only to the training dataset, while validation and test datasets remained unchanged. The test set remained fixed across all experimental stages to avoid data leakage.

**Proposed:**

The dataset was partitioned once, at participant level, into training (846 images), validation (192) and a fixed test set (192), stratified by smile-line group and, within the high smile line group, by reference class. All photographs of a participant remain in a single partition (CLAIM 2024). Augmentation was applied to the training partition only, by the training framework at run time; no augmented copies enter the validation or test sets, and the test set was evaluated once, with the final model. For the millimetre validation, the 145 high-smile-line images with a clinical reference measurement were additionally predicted out of fold in a 5-fold participant-level cross-validation, so that each image was measured from a mask produced by a model that had not seen it.

**Why:** The 70/15/15 → 92/4/4 sequence, the 1,315 → 3,403 count and the unclear partition level are the reviewers' main methodological objection; the count grew through augmentation, and the partition was not at participant level.

**Reviewer item:** R2-5, R2-6, R3-Results-2, R4-7

<!-- source: outputs/07_report/tables/dataset_counts.csv -->

### manuscript · 2.8.1 Preliminary comparison phase

**Current (replace):**

> RF-DETR-Seg was evaluated on dataset v1, whereas YOLOv26 and YOLOv11 were evaluated on datasets v2 and v3, respectively; however, these versions were based on the same baseline dataset configuration and the same split strategy.

**Proposed:**

This stage was a screening step run with the annotation platform's default training settings on separate copies of the same baseline dataset version. Because the training data, preprocessing and settings were not held identical across the three runs, it does not isolate the effect of the architecture and is reported only as the basis for selecting one architecture to take forward; no claim of architectural superiority is made.

**Why:** The reviewer is right that the comparison does not isolate the architecture; the honest fix is to relabel the stage and withdraw the claim.

**Reviewer item:** R4-8

### manuscript · 2.9 Intra-observer calibration

**Current (replace):**

> Intra-observer reliability was assessed on 20 randomly selected images using repeated measurements at different time points. Agreement was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and paired t-tests, demonstrating excellent reliability with high ICC values and no significant differences (p > 0.05).

**Proposed:**

Intra-observer reliability of the clinical reference was assessed by remeasuring the gingival display of 20 images at six tooth sites each, by the same examiner at a separate session: tooth-site level ICC(2,1) 0.995 [0.994, 0.997] (n = 120 tooth-site pairs), image-mean level ICC(2,1) 0.998 [0.995, 0.999] (n = 20 images), mean difference 0.012 [-0.019, 0.042] mm, standard deviation 0.167 mm, 95 % limits of agreement -0.32 to 0.34 mm at tooth-site level. The paired t-test is not used as evidence of agreement; the limits of agreement and the ICC are reported instead.

**Why:** The submitted sentence gives no numbers, cites a paired t-test as evidence of agreement, and calls the repeated measurements 'tooth measurements' although the quantity measured is the gingival display at a tooth site, not a dimension of the tooth. The calibration files used for the original submission contained 15 images per session, not 20; the complete 20-image file was supplied by the clinical team and the statistics were recomputed from it.

**Reviewer item:** R4-4 (reference reliability)

### manuscript · 3.1 (class-wise lip performance)

**Current (replace):**

> In the class-wise evaluation, lip segmentation showed consistently high performance across all models, with class-wise mAP values ranging from 97.0% to 99.0%, whereas gingiva segmentation showed greater variability among architectures. The YOLOv11x-seg model improved mask continuity particularly along the lip-gingiva boundary, reduced the number of fragmented masks, and decreased false-negative rates.

**Proposed:**

On the fixed test set, lip segmentation reached a mask mAP@50 of 0.98 whereas gingiva segmentation reached 0.41. The difference is examined at the boundary rather than left as an aggregate gap: against the annotated masks of the 145 reference images, the upper, lip-side gingiva edge is accurate (mean absolute column-wise error 0.32 mm, bias +0.16 mm) while the lower, festooned gingival margin is placed systematically too low (0.76 mm, bias +0.66 mm); gingiva mask IoU 0.76, lip mask IoU 0.79. Pooled over the whole test set the gingiva IoU is lower (0.51) because in low (0.28) and average (0.49) smile lines the annotated gingiva is thin or absent (median annotated width 16 image columns in the low group against 935 in the high group).

**Why:** The reviewers ask for a quantitative investigation of the lip/gingiva gap and for the low gingiva value to be stated in the text.

**Reviewer item:** R2-8, R2-10

### Appendix B · B.1 (augmentation and splits)

**Current (replace whole paragraph):**

> The dataset was initially divided into 70 % training, 15 % validation, and 15 % test sets. During the hyperparameter optimization phase, an updated dataset version containing 3,403 images was used, with a 92 % training, 4 % validation, and 4 % test split to increase the amount of training data.

Replace the whole paragraph: a single participant-level partition is used; augmentation is applied by the training framework to the training partition at run time (mosaic, scaling, HSV and horizontal flip, with mosaic disabled for the final 10 epochs) and produces no stored image copies; no augmentation is applied to the validation or test images. ## Appendix D

### Appendix D · D.1 (expanded version)

**Current (replace):**

> - Expanded version: Updated dataset used during the hyperparameter optimization phase, containing 3,403 images with a 92% training, 4% validation, and 4% test split. This expanded dataset was specifically used during the hyperparameter optimization phase. In total, 24 hyperparameter combinations were evaluated using a grid-search strategy across batch size [8, 16], epochs [50, 100, 150], initial learning rate [1e-4, 5e-4], and learning-rate decay [0.01, 0.02], with AdamW and cosine learning-rate scheduling held constant.

**Proposed:**

Replace with the final training configuration actually used: dataset 1230 images partitioned at participant level (846 / 192 / 192); model yolo11x-seg.pt; 100 epochs, batch 16, image size 640, AdamW optimiser, initial learning rate 0.0005, final learning-rate fraction 0.02, cosine schedule, close_mosaic 10, patience 20, seed 42, deterministic training; 2.14.0+cu130 / Ultralytics 8.4.153 on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090.

**Why:** The appendix must describe the training that produced the reported model, not the superseded hyperparameter search on an augmented dataset version.

**Reviewer item:** R2-5, R2-9, R4-6, R4-7
